analysis.one_liner: Paused mortgage payments and foreclosure for six months in hurricane disaster areas.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on October 7, 2005, and died there when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, this bill would have frozen all mortgage and commercial real estate loan payments for six months in federally declared disaster areas. Borrowers could not be declared delinquent or in default during that window, no negative information could be reported to credit bureaus, and the six months could not count toward foreclosure timelines. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners, small landlords, nonprofits, and businesses in Katrina and Rita disaster zones whose properties were destroyed or whose income collapsed would get up to six months without mortgage payments, without late fees, credit damage, or foreclosure countdowns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disaster-area homeowners and small property owners

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a six-month moratorium beginning August 28, 2005 on principal and interest payments on loans secured by residential or commercial real estate in presidentially declared Hurricane Katrina and Rita disaster areas [S2][S3].
Bars any covered loan from being declared delinquent or in default during the moratorium, and bars negative reporting to consumer credit bureaus during that period [S2][S3].
Tolls (pauses) all foreclosure and default time clocks, so the six months cannot be counted toward any foreclosure deadline or default period after it ends [S2][S3].
Covers commercial real estate and nonprofit-held property as well as homes, extending protection to small businesses and community organizations in the disaster zone [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, banks, and loan servicers would forgo up to six months of payments on every covered loan in the disaster area and absorb the administrative cost of the freeze, unless Congress separately compensated them (the bill includes no compensation).

drawbacks.text: The moratorium applies to every loan in the disaster area, not only destroyed properties, so lenders and community banks holding performing loans would also lose payments for six months [S3].
The standard “by those who are not in a position to pay” is undefined in the bill, leaving lenders and borrowers without a clear rule for who qualifies [S3].
With no reimbursement mechanism, the cost falls directly on lenders, which critics said could tighten future credit in exactly the regions trying to rebuild.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families whose homes and livelihoods were wiped out, a six-month payment freeze with no credit damage would have been substantial and immediate relief, and it was strictly temporary and tolled so it did not erase debt. The main costs fell on lenders, and the bill's breadth (all loans in the disaster zone, not just damaged ones) and vague eligibility standard were real design weaknesses. On balance it was a targeted, temporary intervention whose cost was concentrated on a well-capitalized industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the bill on October 7, 2005, about six weeks after Hurricane Katrina, and spoke for it on the House floor [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which took no further action on it [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor during the life of the bill [S4].
The 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill was never reported out of committee or brought to a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers were better off: they never had to forgo payments or halt foreclosures in the disaster zone. Disaster-area borrowers got no relief from this bill, though some later received help through other programs outside this bill.

for.name: Rep. Elijah E. Cummings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over mortgage and housing law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 7, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Michael G. Oxley
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee agenda and did not act on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the record shows no party breakdown — only that it died quietly in committee with a Democratic sponsor and no Republican or Democratic co-support [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to forgo up to six months of payments on all loans in the disaster zone and paused foreclosures, without compensation. Its death meant they collected on schedule and continued foreclosures on storm-damaged properties.
The bill barred negative credit reporting on covered loans during the moratorium, reducing the flow of delinquency data they sell to creditors. It never took effect.

industries.industry: Borrowers and communities in disaster areas
industries.note: Homeowners and businesses in the Katrina and Rita zones were the intended beneficiaries. With the bill dead, no moratorium existed and debt obligations continued unchanged.
